newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - EMU minus Italy billed to launch on time.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU minus Italy billed to launch on time.

text.p: A single European currency is on course for its scheduled launch in 1999, but Italy is unlikely to join a core of six founder members, according to a Reuters survey published on Friday.

The poll gave an average prediction that European economic and monetary union (EMU) had an 83 percent chance of getting off the ground on the target date on January 1, 1999, unchanged from the findings of a January survey.
Forty-five economists and think tanks across 15 European countries took part in the survey, which was carried out between February 5 and 6.
"It's getting a bit blustery, but there's no reason to think it's strong enough to blow (EMU) off course," said David Croughan of the Irish Business and Employers' Confederation (IBEC).

Economists were unanimous that the core six -- Austria, the Benelux countries, France and Germany -- would form the launch pad for EMU. Ninety-three percent said Ireland would make the grade too while 80 percent backed Finland.

"The most likely scenario is that EMU will start in 1999 with a relatively small group of countries confined to those north of the Alps," said Georg Busch, international economist at WIFO Research Institute in Vienna.
"Italy, Spain and Portugal will be given a clear perspective of joining one or two years later," added Busch.

The findings will be a dampener to Italy's driving ambitions to join EMU from the outset, which have faltered in recent days by alleged behind-the-scenes moves to keep the lira out for at least a year.
The Financial Times newspaper said on Wednesday that Italy, and possibly Spain and Portugal, would be offered a deal to delay entry until 2000 or 2001.
Italy angrily rejected the idea and Spain and Portugal were quick to quash talk that they would be held ransom to political considerations over Italy's economic fitness.
Nevertheless the survey showed the odds were stacked against Italy, with just seven percent of respondents backing them to join in 1999, compared to 22 percent in the December survey.
February's survey was less dismissive of Spain and Portugal. A third of respondents said Spain would make the first wave, while 29 percent backed Portugal.
The poll showed the odds on Iberian membership shortening. Last October only six and eight percent of analysts thought Spain and Portugal respectively would be in at the start.
"Their performance has improved substantially, but time is running out. A year or two more is needed. They are not mature enough yet," said one economist at a Finnish bank.
Greece, overshooting all of the economic yardsticks for EMU entry, and Britain, dithering on the political front ahead of an election due by May 22, remained the two no-hopers.
Some respondents were less convinced of EMU's infallibility, despite a fresh dose of bullish sentiment on Thursday from EU monetary affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy.

Speaking in southern England, de Silguy said economic convergence and practical preparations towards EMU were firmly on track. He also promised there would be no extra obstacles dreamed up for any countries joining after the first wave.
But some of the experts in the Reuters survey said the sheer enormity of the task could mean the authorities would have to rush to get all the technicalities in place.

"The timing is very tight. There are still decisions to be made on legal issues, bond contracts, all sorts of things. There's still a lot of decision-making to be done," said Bronwyn Curtis, chief economist at Nomura International. She put the chances of EMU going ahead on time at 55 percent.
